meta.title: Personal Protective Equipment in Construction Environments
meta.description: Covers selection, use, fit, inspection, and maintenance of PPE for construction hazards including eye/face, respiratory, head, foot, hand, and body protection under OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart E.

ppe-overview.title: Why PPE Matters in Construction
ppe-overview.content:
Personal protective equipment (PPE) is one of the most visible and important parts of a construction safety program. Construction employees face hazards from falling objects, flying particles, sharp materials, chemicals, dust, fumes, noise, electrical energy, slips, trips, heat, cold, and other jobsite conditions.

Critical principle: PPE does not eliminate hazards — it helps protect the worker when exposure still occurs. A hard hat does not stop objects from falling. Safety glasses do not remove flying particles. Gloves do not make sharp materials harmless. A respirator does not eliminate airborne contaminants. PPE is one layer of protection in a larger safety system that includes engineering controls, safe work practices, and training.

PPE is required when hazards cannot be fully eliminated by other controls or when additional protection is needed. Wearing PPE is not optional when hazards require it.

Common construction hazards that may require PPE:
- Falling, flying, rolling, or swinging objects
- Sharp edges, nails, rebar, and puncture hazards
- Dust, fumes, vapors, gases, mists, or chemical splashes
- Welding light, sparks, molten metal, or intense heat
- Electrical shock or arc hazards
- Noise, vibration, or temperature extremes

ppe-selection-hazard-assessment.title: General PPE Requirements and Hazard Assessment
ppe-selection-hazard-assessment.content:
Before PPE can be selected, hazards must be identified by looking at the task, the tools, the materials, the work area, the environment, and the possible routes of exposure.

OSHA's framework (29 CFR 1910.132 / 1926 Subpart E) requires:
- PPE to be provided, used, and maintained in a reliable and sanitary condition
- PPE appropriate for the hazard must be selected
- Employees must be trained on when PPE is necessary, which PPE is required, how to wear it, and its limitations

PPE selection factors:
- The specific hazard and severity of possible injury
- The body part at risk
- Duration and frequency of exposure
- The work environment and conditions
- Fit and compatibility of multiple PPE items worn together
- Manufacturer instructions and applicable standards
- Whether equipment is damaged, contaminated, expired, or modified

Example: A worker may need safety glasses for general cutting, goggles for heavy dust, and a face shield over eye protection for significant flying particle or chemical splash potential. Choosing PPE is not guesswork — the right protection depends entirely on the hazard.

eye-face-protection.title: Eye and Face Protection
eye-face-protection.content:
The eyes and face are especially vulnerable on construction sites. Flying particles, dust, sparks, chemicals, molten metal, and intense light can cause serious injuries — including permanent vision loss.

Types of eye and face PPE:
- Safety glasses — for flying particle hazards; must have side protection when hazards can approach from the side
- Goggles — provide a seal around the eyes; used for dust, chemical splash, or liquid hazards
- Face shields — protect the face; must be worn OVER primary eye protection, not instead of it
- Welding helmets and filter lenses — required for welding, cutting, and similar operations with intense light/radiation

Important rules:
- A face shield is secondary protection only — safety glasses or goggles are still required underneath
- Inspect eye and face protection before use for: cracked or scratched lenses, missing side shields, broken straps or frames, chemical contamination, poor fit, and missing manufacturer markings

OSHA references: 1910.133 (general industry) / 1926.102 (construction)

respiratory-protection.title: Respiratory Protection
respiratory-protection.content:
Some construction tasks create airborne hazards including dust, mists, fumes, vapors, gases, and other contaminants from cutting concrete, sanding, painting, spraying, demolition, welding, applying chemicals, or working in poor air quality.

Types of respiratory protection:
- Filtering facepiece respirators — protect against certain particles only
- Half-face air-purifying respirators — with cartridges selected for specific contaminants
- Full-face air-purifying respirators — add face protection
- Supplied-air respirators — required in oxygen-deficient or highly hazardous atmospheres

Critical points:
- A filtering facepiece does NOT protect against all chemicals, vapors, gases, or oxygen-deficient atmospheres
- The wrong cartridge may offer NO protection against the hazard — cartridge selection must match the specific contaminant
- Facial hair that interferes with the sealing surface can compromise protection
- A proper seal check must be performed before each use

Before using a respirator, always verify: what airborne hazard is present, which respirator and cartridges are approved for that hazard, and that the respirator fits and seals properly.

OSHA reference: 29 CFR 1910.134

head-protection.title: Head Protection
head-protection.content:
Head injuries can result from falling objects, flying objects, low overhead clearances, electrical contact, or contact with fixed structures. Hard hats and protective helmets reduce the severity of these injuries.

Key distinctions:
- Standard hard hats protect against impact from falling or flying objects
- Electrically rated hard hats also provide protection against electrical contact hazards
- Bump caps protect only against minor bumps in low-clearance areas — they are NOT a substitute for hard hats where falling or flying object hazards exist

Inspect hard hats before use for:
- Cracks, dents, gouges, or holes in the shell
- Brittle or faded shell material
- Damaged suspension system
- Missing adjustment components
- Unauthorized modifications (drilling, painting with incompatible materials)
- Poor fit

A hard hat worn backward without manufacturer approval, modified, or with damaged suspension may not protect as intended. Fit matters — a loose hard hat can fall off during an incident.

OSHA references: 29 CFR 1910.135 / 1926.100

foot-protection.title: Foot Protection
foot-protection.content:
Foot injuries on construction sites can be caused by falling materials, rolling equipment, sharp objects, nails, slippery surfaces, heat, cold, chemicals, or electrical hazards. Safety footwear must be matched to the specific hazard.

Types of foot protection:
- Safety-toe footwear — protects against impact and compression from heavy materials
- Puncture-resistant soles — protects against nails or sharp debris underfoot
- Slip-resistant soles — reduces slips and falls on wet, oily, or uneven surfaces
- Electrical hazard (EH) rated footwear — provides secondary protection against electrical contact
- Insulated footwear — for temperature extremes
- Chemical-resistant boots — for chemical contact hazards
- Waterproof or weather-appropriate footwear — for wet conditions

No single safety shoe protects against every construction hazard. Footwear must be selected based on the specific hazards present and the work surface conditions.

Remove footwear from service when: protective toes are damaged, soles are worn through, holes are present, or the footwear is contaminated with chemicals.

OSHA references: 29 CFR 1910.136 / 1926.96

hand-protection.title: Hand Protection
hand-protection.content:
Hands are used in nearly every construction task and are exposed to cuts, punctures, abrasions, burns, chemicals, vibration, electricity, heat, cold, and crushing hazards. Gloves must be matched to the hazard.

Types of gloves by hazard:
- Cloth gloves — minor abrasions only; NOT appropriate for chemicals or serious cuts
- Leather gloves — rough materials, sparks, and moderate heat
- Cut-resistant gloves — sharp materials such as sheet metal, glass, or rebar
- Chemical-resistant gloves — must be selected for the SPECIFIC chemical; compatibility must be verified
- Heat-resistant gloves — welding, high-temperature surfaces
- Electrical protective gloves — must meet specialized requirements and be inspected per procedures
- Disposable gloves — limited chemical or biological exposure

Fit is critical: gloves that are too loose can snag in machinery; gloves that are too tight reduce circulation and dexterity.

Inspect gloves before use for: holes, tears, cuts, punctures, chemical degradation, stiffness, cracking, contamination, loss of grip, and incorrect glove type for the hazard.

OSHA reference: 29 CFR 1910.138

ppe-fit-maintenance.title: PPE Fit, Maintenance, Storage, and Replacement
ppe-fit-maintenance.content:
Even the right PPE can fail if it does not fit, is not maintained, or is used incorrectly.

Fit requirements (effective January 13, 2025 per 29 CFR 1926 Subpart E update):
- PPE must fit the worker — neither too loose nor too tight
- PPE must stay in place without interfering with movement, vision, communication, breathing, or safe operation of equipment
- Multiple PPE items must be compatible — safety glasses must fit with a respirator; a face shield must not interfere with a hard hat

Maintenance and inspection:
- Inspect PPE before each use
- Damaged, contaminated, expired, altered, or unsanitary PPE must be removed from service immediately
- Do not use cracked face shields, hard hats with damaged suspensions, or gloves left in chemicals (they may degrade and fail silently)
- Clean and store PPE per employer procedures and manufacturer instructions
- Never modify PPE without approval
- Shared PPE must be properly sanitized

When to report:
- PPE that is missing, damaged, contaminated, improperly fitting, or unsuitable for the hazard must be reported immediately
- Employees must not continue work with defective PPE — report it and get suitable replacement before resuming

employer-employee-responsibilities.title: Employee and Employer Responsibilities
employer-employee-responsibilities.content:
PPE safety is a shared responsibility between employers and employees.

Employee responsibilities:
- Wear required PPE whenever jobsite hazards require it
- Use the PPE selected for the specific task and hazard
- Inspect PPE before use
- Adjust PPE for proper fit
- Keep PPE clean, sanitary, and properly stored
- Follow training and manufacturer instructions
- Report damaged, missing, contaminated, or poorly fitting PPE
- Never modify PPE in a way that reduces protection
- Ask questions when unsure which PPE is required

Employer responsibilities:
- Identify jobsite hazards requiring PPE and conduct hazard assessments
- Select PPE appropriate for each hazard and ensure it fits properly
- Provide and maintain required PPE in a sanitary, reliable condition
- Train employees on when PPE is needed and how to use it correctly
- Retrain employees when conditions, equipment, or performance indicate a need
- Enforce PPE use consistently and replace damaged or unsuitable PPE
- Ensure compatibility when multiple PPE items are worn together
- Maintain documentation as required

If PPE does not fit, is uncomfortable, interferes with the task, or does not seem right for the hazard — the solution is not to skip it. The solution is to get the correct PPE, correct fit, or additional instruction.
